title: Properties of Substances: Melting and Boiling Points, Gases, Conductors
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Chemistry
summary: Melting and boiling points as properties, how to find the state of a substance at any temperature, why gases have mass, and electrical and thermal conductors and insulators.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that the temperature at which a substance changes state (its melting point and boiling point) is a **property** of that substance (6Cp.01)
Know that **gases** have properties, including **mass** (6Cp.02)
Understand that **electrical conductivity** and **thermal conductivity** are properties of a substance (6Cp.03)

blocks.text: 1. What is a property?

A **property** is something that describes what a substance is like or how it behaves — for example its colour, hardness, whether it is magnetic, whether it floats. A property is the same every time for that substance: pure copper always conducts electricity; pure water always boils at the same temperature at normal air pressure. Scientists use properties to **identify** substances and to **choose** the right material for a job.

items: property
خاصية — what a substance is like or how it behaves
melting point
درجة الانصهار — the temperature at which a solid melts (or a liquid freezes)
boiling point
درجة الغليان — the temperature at which a liquid boils
state of matter
حالة المادة — solid, liquid or gas
mass
الكتلة — how much matter something has; measured in g or kg
electrical conductor / insulator
موصل / عازل للكهرباء
thermal conductor / insulator
موصل / عازل للحرارة
particle
جسيم — a tiny piece that all substances are made of

blocks.text: 2. Melting point and boiling point

The **melting point** is the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. The same temperature is the **freezing point** (liquid → solid). The **boiling point** is the temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into a gas quickly. Each substance has its **own** melting point and boiling point — that is why they are properties.

rows: liquid (the only metal that is liquid at room temperature)

blocks.text: **How to work out the state at any temperature** — compare the temperature with the melting point (mp) and the boiling point (bp):

items: Temperature **lower than** the mp → **solid**.
Temperature **between** the mp and the bp → **liquid**.
Temperature **higher than** the bp → **gas**.

blocks.title: Careful with negative numbers
blocks.text: −114 is **lower** (colder) than −39, because it is further below zero. Draw a quick number line if you are unsure. Example: at −50 °C, is mercury solid or liquid? −50 is lower than −39 (its mp), so mercury is **solid**.

**Using melting point to test purity:** pure water freezes at exactly 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. If salt is dissolved in it, it freezes below 0 °C and boils above 100 °C. So if a 'water' sample boils at 103 °C, it is not pure water. (This is why salt is spread on icy roads in cold countries.)

blocks.title: بالعربي: القاعدة الذهبية
blocks.text: كل مادة ليها درجة انصهار (melting point) ودرجة غليان (boiling point) خاصة بيها، وده اسمه خاصية (property). لو درجة الحرارة أقل من درجة الانصهار ← صلب solid. بين الانصهار والغليان ← سائل liquid. أعلى من الغليان ← غاز gas. وخلي بالك: ‎−114 أبرد من ‎−39.
3. Gases have properties — including mass

Gases are hard to notice because most are invisible, but they are real substances made of **particles**, just like solids and liquids. In a gas the particles are **far apart** and move quickly in all directions.

blocks.text: Each gas particle has a tiny mass, so a gas has mass. One litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 g — small, but it can be measured on a sensitive balance. Another example: an unopened bottle of fizzy drink has a greater mass than the same bottle after it has been opened and left to go flat, because carbon dioxide gas has escaped.

blocks.title: "Air is nothing" — wrong!
blocks.text: A container 'full of air' is not empty. Air is a mixture of gases (mainly nitrogen and oxygen) and it has mass and takes up space.
4. Electrical and thermal conductivity

**Electrical conductivity** describes whether a substance lets electricity pass through it. An **electrical conductor** lets electricity flow; an **electrical insulator** does not. **Thermal conductivity** describes whether a substance lets heat (thermal energy) pass through it easily. A **thermal conductor** lets heat pass quickly; a **thermal insulator** slows heat down. Both are properties: they depend on what the substance is.

rows: all metals (copper, aluminium, iron, steel, gold, silver); graphite (pencil 'lead') — a non-metal that conducts
plastic, rubber, wood, glass, dry paper, fabric, air
plastic, wood, wool, polystyrene, glass, air

blocks.text: **Testing electrical conductivity:** put the material in the gap of a simple circuit. If the lamp lights, the material is an electrical conductor.

blocks.text: 5. Investigation: which metal is the best thermal conductor?

Rods of different materials were stood in a beaker of hot water. A small bead was stuck to the top of each rod with wax. When heat travels up the rod, the wax melts and the bead falls. The time for each bead to fall was measured.

items: **Independent variable:** the material of the rod. **Dependent variable:** the time for the bead to fall.
**Control variables:** same length and thickness of rod, same temperature of water, same amount of wax, same size of bead, same depth in the water.
**Conclusion:** copper is the best thermal conductor (shortest time); glass is a thermal insulator.
**Risk:** hot water can scald — stand the beaker on a flat surface, do not lean over it, and let rods cool before touching.

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Substance X melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C. What is its state at (a) −20 °C (b) 25 °C (c) 80 °C? [3 marks]

items: (a) −20 is lower than −7 (the mp) → **solid**.
(b) 25 is between −7 and 59 → **liquid**.
(c) 80 is higher than 59 (the bp) → **gas**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** thinking −20 is 'higher' than −7 because 20 is bigger than 7.
**Worked example 2** — Use the table of substances. Which substance has a boiling point 22 °C lower than water's? [1 mark]
**Answer:** 100 − 22 = 78 °C, which is the boiling point of **ethanol**.

**Worked example 3** — Mona weighs a bottle of fizzy water: 520 g. She opens it, leaves it overnight, puts the lid back on and weighs it again: 516 g. (a) What mass of gas escaped? (b) What does this show about gases? [2 marks]

items: (b) The gas (carbon dioxide) that escaped had mass — **gases have mass**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Explain why the handle of a saucepan is made of plastic but the base is made of metal. [2 marks]

**Answer:** the metal base is a good thermal conductor, so heat passes quickly to the food (1); plastic is a thermal insulator, so the handle does not get too hot to hold (1). **Common mistake:** writing 'plastic does not conduct electricity' — the question is about **heat**.
**Worked example 5** — Omar tests a pencil lead (graphite) in the conductivity tester and the lamp lights. He says, "Graphite must be a metal." Is he correct? [1 mark]
**Answer:** No — graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity. Most non-metals are insulators, but graphite is an exception.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up melting point and boiling point when working out a state — write 'mp' and 'bp' next to the numbers first.
Getting negative temperatures the wrong way round (−50 °C is colder than −10 °C).
Saying gases 'weigh nothing' or 'are empty space'. Gases have mass.
Confusing **electrical** and **thermal** conductivity. Read the question: electricity or heat?
Saying 'all metals are magnetic' or 'all non-metals are insulators' — iron is magnetic but copper is not; graphite conducts.
Saying wood or plastic 'stops heat completely'. Insulators **slow down** heat flow.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: A **table of melting and boiling points**: give the state of a substance at a stated temperature, or say which substance is a gas/liquid at room temperature.
**Calculate** a difference: a temperature difference, or a change in mass (e.g. a ball before and after pumping). Show the subtraction.
**Explain** a choice of material using the words conductor / insulator and electrical / thermal.
**Investigation**: name variables, read a results table, choose the best conductor, suggest a control variable or a safety precaution.
Complete or read a **circuit** used to test conductivity — know the symbols for a cell and a lamp.

questions.q: (b) Which substance, A, B or C, is a gas at 20 °C?
questions.e: 20 °C is higher than A's bp (−183 °C), so A is a gas. B is liquid and C is solid at 20 °C.

questions.p:

The table gives melting points (mp) and boiling points (bp).
Substance A: mp −218 °C, bp −183 °C
Substance B: mp −39 °C, bp 357 °C
Substance C: mp 1538 °C, bp 2862 °C
questions.q: (c) What is the state of substance C at 1600 °C?
questions.e: 1600 is higher than 1538 (mp) but lower than 2862 (bp), so C is a liquid.

questions.q: (d) What is the state of substance B at −50 °C?
questions.e: −50 °C is lower (colder) than B's mp of −39 °C, so B is a solid.

questions.q: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water boils at 100 °C. How many degrees higher is the boiling point of water?
Which statement shows that melting point is a **property** of a substance?
c: Ice cubes melt faster in a warm room.
Big pieces of ice take longer to melt.
Ice melts when you hold it.
questions.e: A property is the same every time for that substance. Pure ice always melts at the same temperature, 0 °C. The other statements are about how fast melting happens.

questions.q: (a) What is the mass of the air that was pumped in?

questions.p:
Question 7
A flat ball has a mass of 432 g. It is pumped up with air and weighed again. Its mass is now 439 g.
questions.q: (b) What does this experiment show about air? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: air / gas has mass. 1 mark: the mass increased when only air was added. Do not accept 'air is heavy' alone.
questions.e: Air (a gas) has mass: the only thing added to the ball was air, and the mass went up by 7 g.
Steel is a metal, so it conducts electricity. Plastic, rubber and glass are insulators.

questions.q: Electrical wires have copper in the middle and a plastic coating. Explain why each material is used.
questions.ms: 1 mark: copper is a (good) electrical conductor, so electricity flows through it. 1 mark: plastic is an electrical insulator, so it stops electricity reaching the user / stops electric shocks. Do not accept 'plastic is a thermal insulator'.
questions.e: Copper is a good electrical conductor, so it carries the electricity. Plastic is an electrical insulator, so it keeps the electricity in the wire and protects people from shocks.

questions.p:
Question 11
Rods of four materials were stood in hot water. A bead was stuck to the top of each rod with wax.
Time for the bead to fall:
copper 35 s
aluminium 55 s
steel 140 s
glass — did not fall in 10 minutes
questions.q: (a) Which material is the best thermal conductor?
questions.e: Copper: its bead fell first (35 s), so heat travelled through it fastest.

questions.q: (c) Give **two** variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair test.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, any two: length of the rods; thickness of the rods; temperature of the water; amount of wax; size/mass of the bead; depth of the rod in the water / volume of water. Do not accept 'the material' (this is the independent variable) or 'the time' (dependent variable).
questions.e: For example: the same length and thickness of rod, and the same starting temperature of the water.

questions.q: Which is a property of **all** gases?
questions.e: All gases have mass. Gases have no fixed shape, can be squashed (compressed), and most are invisible.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Each substance has its own **melting point** and **boiling point** — these are properties.
Below mp → solid; between mp and bp → liquid; above bp → gas. Watch negative numbers.
Gases are made of particles that are far apart; gases fill containers, can be squashed, flow and **have mass**.
Metals and graphite conduct **electricity**; plastic, rubber, wood, glass and air are electrical insulators.
Metals are good **thermal** conductors; plastic, wood, wool and trapped air are thermal insulators.
